newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Outrage over slow world response to Zaire crisis.
newsitem.headline: Outrage over slow world response to Zaire crisis.

text.p: Pressure intensified on the United Nations and world powers to speed up their confused plan for a rescue mission to save more than a million war refugees in Zaire.
The U.N.'s Security Council decided on Saturday to deploy a multinational force but its failure to state when or how it should go in was greeted with outrage in the humanitarian community.

Europe's top humanitarian official termed the U.N. inaction a scandal. France, which initiated the plan, pressed for early intervention, and the United States, moved by the unfolding calamity in Zaire, leaned cautiously towards action.

"There is an emerging international consensus that humanitarian intervention will be necessary to address the crisis in eastern Zaire," a senior U.S. official, who asked not to be identified, told Reuters.
"There is also an emerging consensus that to be effective a humanitarian intervention will require a security component," the official said.

"We are actively studying what type of security component would be necessary for an intervention. We are also actively studying what role the U.S. might play as part of such a security component," the official said.

Both the United States and sponsor France are permanent members of the Security Council, whose failure to authorise immediate intervention in Zaire enraged those warning of catastrophe unless food, water and medicine is rushed to the refugees and east Zaireans caught up in a three-week rebellion.

"Those governments who have prevented the immediate authorisation of a multinational protection force should explain to their citizens and the world why," European Commissioner Emma Bonino thundered in Brussels.
But diplomats said the United States, Britain and Russia all had grave reservations about the French-backed plan.
"What are the intentions? What are you going to do? Who are the bad guys and how are you going to separate them from the good guys?" asked a senior diplomat in central Africa.

In Goma, the biggest east Zaire city captured by rebels in a growing insurrection against President Mobutu Sese Seko, Red Cross officials predicted disaster and some 120 exhausted, hungry refugees arrived after walking for more than a week.
Rioting Zaireans seized the last food from a U.N. warehouse.

A German aid mission brought some hope on Saturday, delivering the first medical supplies to reach Goma since rebels captured the city just over a week ago. Ethnic Tutsi rebels have seized Zaire's two eastern provinces since October 18.

Rwanda and the rebels it supports have both rejected any French role in a multinational force, citing France's long alliances with Mobutu and the former Rwandan Hutu leaders who ordered the genocide of minority Tutsis in 1994.
Rwanda's backing for any move to help the needy is vital. The only other corridor is through Zaire, which says the 1.2 million Hutu refugees from Rwanda and Burundi must leave.
France urged the United Nations on Saturday to act as fast as possible to set up an international force and appealed to the United States to contribute a third of the troops.
"This is an important step which we hope will lead as soon as possible to a new decision by the Security Council for its effective implementation," A French government statement said.
U.N. envoy Raymond Chretien apparently failed in talks in Kinshasa to persuade Zairean authorities to agree to safe havens inside Zaire for the Rwandan and Burundian refugees.

"The government took a firm decision yesterday that food destined for the refugees should be distributed in Rwanda to facilitate the return of the refugees to their country of origin," Zairean Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo told reporters.
